readerTitle: Same business, two prices: why valuations swing
caseNote: 가상 사례 (회계 사무소, 식당 그룹) + 실제 연구 (Shiller 1981) + 실제 관찰 (2022년 금리 상승기 성장주 하락)
insight: 가치평가가 크게 흔들리는 것은 사업이 바뀌어서가 아니라, 먼 미래에 대한 작은 가정이 바뀌기 때문이다. 숫자 하나보다 범위와 가정을 본다.
misconception: 가치가 크게 달라졌다면 둘 중 하나가 틀렸거나 사업 자체가 나빠진(좋아진) 것이다.

sources.text: Shiller, R. J. (1981). Do Stock Prices Move Too Much to be Justified by Subsequent Changes in Dividends? American Economic Review, 71(3), 421–436.
성장 영구연금 공식 (가치 = 연간 현금 ÷ (요구수익률 − 성장률)), 재무관리 표준 개념
회계 사무소와 식당 그룹 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 처음 10년 현금의 현재가치 비중(요구수익률 12%, 성장률 4%): (1.04/1.12)^10 ≈ 0.477, 따라서 처음 10년 ≈ $2.5M × (1 − 0.477) ≈ $1.31M ≈ 52%. 카드에는 "about half of the value comes after year 10"으로 적음.
Shiller(1981)는 주가 변동이 이후 실제 배당 변화로 설명되는 수준보다 훨씬 크다는 결과를 제시함. 카드에는 일반적 표현으로만 적음. 게시 전 원문 요지 재확인.
2022년 금리 급등기에 수익이 나지 않는 고성장 기술주가 안정적 기업보다 대체로 더 크게 하락했다는 일반적 관찰. 구체 수치는 넣지 않음. 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인.

cards.title: Same business, two prices: why valuations swing
body: Dana runs a bookkeeping firm. It brings in about $200,000 of cash a year, every year, for twenty clients who rarely leave.
In the same month, two buyers make offers. One says $2.0 million. The other says $3.3 million. Same books. Same clients. Same Dana.

image.label: Two offer letters with very different numbers on one desk
image.brief: 사무실 책상 위에 봉투 두 장이 놓여 있고, 한 장에는 "$2.0M", 다른 한 장에는 "$3.3M"이 크게 적혀 있음. 가운데에 같은 장부 한 권. 차분한 일러스트 톤, 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: Why are the offers so far apart?
body: Both buyers saw the same financials. Neither is a fool. Dana wants to understand the gap before she replies.
What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: One buyer made a math mistake
options.feedback: Possible, but unlikely with careful buyers. Assuming an error means Dana learns nothing about what each buyer believes.

options.text: They disagree a little about future growth and risk
options.feedback: Right. Small differences in what they expect, and what return they need, add up to a very big gap. The next card shows how.

options.text: The higher buyer found extra profit Dana missed
options.feedback: Worth asking, but the cash is the same for both. The gap comes from the future each buyer imagines, not from today's numbers.

cards.title: Same $200,000. Three different futures.

breakdown.label: Buyer A
breakdown.detail: Wants a 12% yearly return, expects 2% growth

cards.callout: A simple rule of thumb: value ≈ yearly cash ÷ (return the buyer needs − expected growth). Two points of difference moved the price by about 67%.

cards.title: Valuations rest on the far future
body: A valuation is today's price for all the cash a business will make in the future. Most of that cash is years away, so the number depends on guesses about growth and risk.

That makes value **sensitive to assumptions**. In Dana's middle case, about half of the value comes from cash earned after year 10. Nudge the guess about those distant years, and the whole price moves.
The business did not change. The view of its future did.

image.label: Bar of yearly cash stretching into the distance
image.brief: 가로로 길게 이어지는 연도별 현금 막대. 앞의 10년 막대는 진하고, 10년 이후 막대는 점점 흐려지며 멀리까지 이어짐. "Years 1–10: about half", "After year 10: about half" 라벨.

cards.title: Prices move more than businesses do.
body: In 1981, economist Robert Shiller compared stock prices with the dividends companies actually paid later. Prices swung far more than those later payouts could justify.
His point was not that markets are silly. It was that prices track *expectations*, and expectations move faster than real cash.
The same thing happens in private deals. A buyer's mood, interest rates and recent news all shift the inputs, even when the business sits still.

cards.title: Fast growers swing the hardest.
body: The closer expected growth gets to the return a buyer needs, the more each point matters. A steady business with low growth barely moves when rates change. A fast grower can lose a big share of its value from a small change in rates.
That is why, when interest rates rose sharply in 2022, fast-growing companies with no profits yet generally fell much harder than steady ones.
cards.softwareNote: A software company valued on growth expected years from now is mostly far-future cash. A small cut in its growth forecast, or a rise in rates, can move its valuation far more than this quarter's results would suggest.

cards.title: Swings don't make valuation useless.
body: A number that moves is still useful if you know what moves it. Treat a valuation as a **range**, tied to clear assumptions, not a single truth.

Beware of picking the growth rate that gives the number you want. And the shortcut on card 3 breaks when expected growth gets close to the required return. The math then explodes, which is a sign the assumptions, not the business, are doing the work.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant group.
body: You own four restaurants and want to sell a 20% stake to an investor. Profit rose 10% this year. Yet the investor's valuation is 25% lower than one you heard last year.

options.text: Assume the business got worse and start cutting costs
options.feedback: Profit actually went up. Cutting costs to fix a problem that isn't in the business could hurt service and the very growth investors want.

options.text: Ask which assumption changed, then test a range yourself
options.feedback: If the investor now needs a higher return or expects slower growth, you can argue the inputs, show evidence, or decide the timing is wrong.

options.text: Refuse and wait, since valuations always bounce back
options.feedback: Waiting can be wise if rates or mood drove the drop. But without knowing why, you may wait for a recovery that never comes.

cards.title: A valuation is a view of the future, not a fact about today.
body: When a value jumps or drops, ask which assumption changed before asking what changed in the business.
**Try it today:** estimate your business's yearly cash. Divide it by 8%, then by 6%. Notice how far apart the two answers are, and why.
